{{short description|Quantum state of multiple particles represented as complex matrices}}
[[File:Matrix product state obc tikz.svg|right|250px|thumb|For periodic boundary conditions,[[Penrose graphical notation]] (tensor diagram notation) of a matrix product state of five particles.]]

A '''matrix product state (MPS)''' is a representation of a quantum many-body state. It is at the core of the [[density matrix renormalization group]] (DMRG) algorithm.

For a system of <math>N</math> spins of dimension <math>d</math>, the general form of the MPS for [[periodic boundary conditions]] (PBC) can be written in the following form:
[[File:Mps_open_bc_500dpi.png|thumb|For open boundary conditions, [[Penrose graphical notation]] (tensor diagram notation) of a matrix product state of five particles.]]
<math display="block">|\Psi\rangle = \sum_{\{s\}} \operatorname{Tr}\left[A_1^{(s_1)} A_2^{(s_2)} \cdots A_N^{(s_N)}\right] |s_1 s_2 \ldots s_N\rangle.</math> 

For open boundary conditions (OBC), <math>|\Psi\rangle</math> takes the form

:<math>|\Psi\rangle = \sum_{\{s\}} A_1^{(s_1)} A_2^{(s_2)} \cdots A_N^{(s_N)} |s_1 s_2 \ldots s_N\rangle.</math>

Here <math>
A_i^{(s_i)}
</math> are the <math>D_i\times D_{i+1}</math> matrices (<math>D</math> is the dimension of the virtual subsystems) and <math>|s_i\rangle</math> are the single-site basis states.  For periodic boundary conditions, we consider <math>D_{N+1}=D_1</math>,  and for open boundary conditions <math>D_1=1</math>. The parameter <math>D</math>  is related to the [[Quantum entanglement|entanglement]] between particles. In particular, if the state is a [[product state]] (i.e. not entangled at all), it can be described as a matrix product state with <math>D=1</math>. <math>\{s_i\}</math> represents a <math>d</math>-dimensional local space on site <math>i=1,2,...,N</math>.  For [[Qubit|qubits]], <math>s_i\in \{0,1\}</math>. For qudits (''{{mvar|d}}''-level systems), <math>s_i\in \{0,1,\ldots,d-1\}</math>.

For states that are translationally symmetric, we can choose: <math display="block">
A_1^{(s)} = A_2^{(s)} = \cdots = A_N^{(s)} \equiv A^{(s)}.
</math> In general, every state can be written in the MPS form (with <math>D</math> growing exponentially with the particle number ''{{mvar|N}}''). Note that the MPS decomposition is not unique. MPS are practical when <math>D</math>  is small – for example, does not depend on the [[particle number]]. Except for a small number of specific cases (some mentioned in the section [[#Examples|Examples]]), such a thing is not possible, though in many cases it serves as a good approximation.

For introductions see,<ref name="PerezGarcia:2006" /><ref name="Orus:2014" /><ref name="Verstraete:2008" /> and.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bridgeman |first1=Jacob C |last2=Chubb |first2=Christopher T |date=2017-06-02 |title=Hand-waving and interpretive dance: an introductory course on tensor networks |url=https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1751-8121/aa6dc3 |journal=Journal of Physics A: Mathematical and Theoretical |volume=50 |issue=22 |page=223001 |doi=10.1088/1751-8121/aa6dc3 |arxiv=1603.03039 |bibcode=2017JPhA...50v3001B |issn=1751-8113}}</ref> In the context of finite automata see.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Crosswhite |first1=Gregory M. |last2=Bacon |first2=Dave |date=2008-07-29 |title=Finite automata for caching in matrix product algorithms |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevA.78.012356 |journal=Physical Review A |language=en |volume=78 |issue=1 |article-number=012356 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevA.78.012356 |arxiv=0708.1221 |bibcode=2008PhRvA..78a2356C |issn=1050-2947}}</ref> For emphasis placed on the graphical reasoning of tensor networks, see the introduction.<ref name="Biamonte:2018" />

== Wave function as a matrix product state ==
For a system of <math>N</math> lattice sites each of which has a <math>d</math>-dimensional [[Hilbert space]], the completely general state can be written as

:<math>|\Psi\rangle = \sum_{\{s\}} \psi_{s_1...s_N} |s_1 \ldots s_N\rangle ,</math>

where <math>\psi_{s_1...s_N}</math> is a <math>d^N</math>-dimensional tensor. For example, the wave function of the system described by the [[Quantum Heisenberg model|Heisenberg model]] is defined by the <math>2^N</math> dimensional tensor, whereas for the [[Hubbard model]] the rank is <math>4^N</math>.

The main idea of the MPS approach is to separate physical degrees of freedom of each site, so that the wave function can be rewritten as the product of <math>N</math> matrices, where each matrix corresponds to one particular site. The whole procedure includes the series of reshaping and [[Singular value decomposition|singular value decompositions]] (SVD).<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Baker |first1=Thomas E. |last2=Desrosiers |first2=Samuel |last3=Tremblay |first3=Maxime |last4=Thompson |first4=Martin P. |title=Méthodes de calcul avec réseaux de tenseurs en physique |url=https://cdnsciencepub.com/doi/10.1139/cjp-2019-0611 |journal=Canadian Journal of Physics |date=2021 |language=en |volume=99 |issue=4 |pages=207–221 |doi=10.1139/cjp-2019-0611 |arxiv=1911.11566 |bibcode=2021CaJPh..99..207B |issn=0008-4204}}</ref><ref>{{Citation |last1=Baker |first1=Thomas E. |title=Build your own tensor network library: DMRjulia I. Basic library for the density matrix renormalization group |date=2021-09-07 |arxiv=2109.03120 |last2=Thompson |first2=Martin P.}}</ref>

There are three ways to represent wave function as an MPS: left-canonical decomposition, right-canonical decomposition, and mixed-canonical decomposition.<ref name="Schollwoeck:2011" />

=== Left-canonical decomposition ===
The decomposition of the <math>d^N</math>-dimensional tensor starts with the separation of the very left index, i.e., the first index <math>s_1</math>, which describes physical degrees of freedom of the first site. It is performed by reshaping <math>|\Psi\rangle</math> as follows

:<math>|\Psi\rangle = \sum_{\{s\}} \psi_{s_1, (s_2...s_N )} |s_1 \ldots s_N\rangle. </math>

In this notation, <math>s_1 </math> is treated as a row index, <math>( s_2 \ldots s_N) </math> as a column index, and the coefficient <math>\psi_{s_1,(s_2...s_N )}</math> is of dimension <math>(d \times d^{N-1})</math>. The SVD procedure yields

:<math>\psi_{s_1,(s_2...s_N )} = \sum_{\alpha_1}^{r_1} U_{s_1,\alpha_1} D_{\alpha_1,\alpha_1} (V^{\dagger})_{\alpha_1,(s_2...s_N )} = \sum_{\alpha_1}^{r_1} U_{s_1,\alpha_1}\psi_{\alpha_1, (s_2...s_N )} = \sum^{r_1}_{\alpha_1} A^{s_1}_{\alpha_1} \psi_{\alpha_1,(s_2...s_N )}.</math>
[[File:Left_mps_1.png|thumb|351x351px|The separation of physical degrees of freedom of the first site.]]
In the relation above, matrices <math>D </math> and <math>V^{\dagger} </math> are multiplied and form the matrix <math>\psi_{\alpha_1,(s_2...s_N )} </math> and <math>r_1 \leq d</math>. <math>A^{s_1}_{\alpha_1}</math> stores the information about the first lattice site. It was obtained by decomposing matrix <math>U</math> into <math>d</math> row vectors <math>A^{s_1}</math> with entries <math>A^{s_1}_{\alpha_1}=U_{s_1,\alpha_1} </math>. So, the state vector takes the form

:<math>|\Psi\rangle = \sum_{\{s\}} \sum_{\alpha_1} A^{s_1}_{\alpha_1} \psi_{\alpha_1,(s_2...s_N )} |s_1 \ldots s_N\rangle.</math>

The separation of the second site is performed by grouping <math>s_2</math> and <math>\alpha_1</math>, and representing  <math>\psi_{\alpha_1,(s_2...s_N )} </math> as a matrix  <math>\psi_{(\alpha_1 s_2),(s_3...s_N )}</math> of dimension <math>(r_1 d \times d^{N-2})</math>. The subsequent SVD of <math>\psi_{(\alpha_1 s_2),(s_3...s_N )}</math> can be performed as follows:

:<math>\psi_{ (\alpha_1 s_2), (s_3...s_N ) } = \sum^{r_2}_{\alpha_2} U_{ (\alpha_1 s_2), \alpha_2} D_{\alpha_2,\alpha_2} (V^{\dagger})_{\alpha_2,(s_3 ... s_N)} = \sum^{r_2}_{\alpha_2} A^{s_2}_{\alpha_1,\alpha_2}\psi_{\alpha_2,(s_3 ... s_N)}</math>.
[[File:Left_mps_2.png|thumb|431x431px|The separation of physical degrees of freedom for the first two sites.]]
Above we replace <math>U</math> by a set of <math>d</math> matrices of dimension <math>(r_1 \times r_2)</math> with entries <math>A^{s_2}_{\alpha_1,\alpha_2} = U_{ (\alpha_1 s_2), \alpha_2}</math>. The dimension of <math>\psi_{\alpha_2,(s_3 ... s_N)}</math> is <math>(r_2 \times d^{N-2})</math> with <math>r_2 \leq r_1 d \leq d^2</math>.  Hence,

:<math>|\Psi\rangle = \sum_{\{s\}} \sum_{\alpha_1} A^{s_1}_{\alpha_1} \psi_{(\alpha_1 s_2),(s_3...s_N )} |s_1 \ldots s_N\rangle = \sum_{\{s\}} \sum_{\alpha_1, \alpha_2} A^{s_1}_{\alpha_1} A^{s_2}_{\alpha_1, \alpha_2} \psi_{\alpha_2,(s_3...s_N )} |s_1 \ldots s_N\rangle.</math>

Following the steps described above, the state <math>|\Psi\rangle</math> can be represented as a product of matrices

:<math>|\Psi\rangle =\sum_{\{s\}} \sum_{\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_{N-1}} A^{s_1}_{\alpha_1} A^{s_2}_{\alpha_1,\alpha_2}\ldots A^{s_{N-1}}_{\alpha_{N-2},\alpha_{N-1}} A^{s_N}_{\alpha_{N-1}} |s_1 \ldots s_N\rangle.</math>

The maximal dimensions of the <math>A</math>-matrices take place in the case of the exact decomposition, i.e., assuming for simplicity that <math>N</math> is even, <math>(1\times d),(d\times d^2),\ldots,(d^{N/2-1}\times d^{N/2}),(d^{N/2}\times d^{N/2-1}),\ldots,(d^2\times d),(d\times 1)</math> going from the first to the last site. However, due to the [[exponential growth]] of the matrix dimensions in most of the cases it is impossible to perform the exact decomposition.

The dual MPS is defined by replacing each matrix <math>A</math> with <math>A^*</math>:

:<math>\langle\Psi|
    =\sum\limits_{\{s\}}\sum\limits_{\alpha'_1,...,\alpha'_{N-1}}A^{*s'_1}_{\alpha'_1}A^{*s'_2}_{\alpha'_1,\alpha'_2}...A^{*s'_{N-1}}_{\alpha'_{N-2},\alpha'_{N-1}}A^{*s'_{N}}_{\alpha'_{N-1}}\langle s'_1...s'_N|.</math>

Note that each matrix <math>U</math> in the SVD is a [[Semi-orthogonal matrix|semi-unitary matrix]] with property <math>U^\dagger U = I</math>. This leads to

:<math>\delta_{\alpha_i,\alpha_j} = \sum_{\alpha_{i-1}s_i} (U^\dagger)_{\alpha_i, (\alpha_{i-1}s_i)} U_{(\alpha_{i-1}s_i), \alpha_j} = \sum_{\alpha_{i-1}s_i} (A^{s_i \dagger})_{\alpha_i, \alpha_{i-1}} A^{s_i}_{\alpha_{i-1}, \alpha_j} = \sum_{s_i} (A^{s_i \dagger} A^{s_i})_{\alpha_i, \alpha_j}</math>.

To be more precise, <math>\sum_{s_i} A^{s_i \dagger} A^{s_i} = I</math>. Since matrices are left-normalized, we call the composition left-canonical.

=== Right-canonical decomposition ===
Similarly, the decomposition can be started from the very right site. After the separation of the first index, the tensor  <math>\psi_{s_1...s_N}</math> transforms as follows:

:<math>\psi_{s_1...s_N} = \psi_{(s_1 ... s_{N-1}),s_N} = \sum_{\alpha_{N-1}} U_{(s_1 ... s_{N-1}),\alpha_{N-1}} D_{\alpha_{N-1},\alpha_{N-1}}(V^\dagger)_{\alpha_{N-1}, s_N} = \sum_{\alpha_{N-1}} \psi_{(s_1 ... s_{N-1}),\alpha_{N-1}} B^{s_N}_{\alpha_{N-1}}</math>.

The matrix <math>\psi_{(s_1 ... s_{N-1}),\alpha_{N-1}}</math> was obtained by multiplying matrices <math>U</math> and <math>D</math>, and the reshaping of <math>(V^\dagger)_{\alpha_{N-1}, s_N}</math> into <math>d</math> column vectors forms <math>B^{s_N}_{\alpha_{N-1}}</math>. Performing the series of reshaping and SVD, the state vector takes the form

:<math>|\Psi\rangle =\sum_{\{s\}} \sum_{\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_{N-1}} B^{s_1}_{\alpha_1} B^{s_2}_{\alpha_1,\alpha_2}\ldots B^{s_{N-1}}_{\alpha_{N-2},\alpha_{N-1}} B^{s_N}_{\alpha_{N-1}} |s_1 \ldots s_N\rangle.</math>

Since each matrix <math>V</math> in the SVD is a [[Semi-orthogonal matrix|semi-unitary matrix]] with property <math>V^\dagger V = I</math>, the <math>B</math>-matrices are right-normalized and obey <math>\sum_{s_i} B^{s_i} B^{s_i \dagger} = I</math>.  Hence, the decomposition is called right-canonical.

=== Mixed-canonical decomposition ===
The decomposition performs from both the right and from the left. Assuming that the left-canonical decomposition was performed for the first n sites,  <math>\psi_{s_1...s_N}</math> can be rewritten as

:<math>\psi_{s_1...s_N} = \sum_{\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_{n}} A^{s_1}_{\alpha_1} A^{s_2}_{\alpha_1,\alpha_2}\ldots A^{s_{n}}_{\alpha_{n-1},\alpha_{n}} D_{\alpha_n, \alpha_n} (V^\dagger)_{\alpha_n, (s_{n+1}...s_N)}</math>.
[[File:Mixed_mps.png|thumb|490x490px|MPS representation obtained by the mixed-canonical decomposition.]]
In the next step, we reshape <math>(V^\dagger)_{\alpha_n, (s_{n+1}...s_N)} </math> as <math>\psi_{(\alpha_n s_{n+1} ... s_{n-1}), s_N}</math> and proceed with the series of reshaping and SVD from the right up to site <math>s_{n+1} </math>:

:<math>\begin{align}
\psi_{(\alpha_n s_{n+1} ... s_{n-1}), s_N} =& \sum_{\alpha_{n+1} ... \alpha_N} U_{(\alpha_n s_{n+1}), \alpha_{n+1}} D_{\alpha_{n+1}, \alpha_{n+1}}B^{s_{n+2}}_{\alpha_{n+1},\alpha_{n+2}}\ldots B^{s_{N-1}}_{\alpha_{N-2},\alpha_{N-1}} B^{s_N}_{\alpha_{N-1}} \\
 =& \sum_{\alpha_{n+1} ... \alpha_N} B^{s_{n+1}}_{\alpha_n, \alpha_{n+1}} B^{s_{n+2}}_{\alpha_{n+1},\alpha_{n+2}}\ldots B^{s_{N-1}}_{\alpha_{N-2},\alpha_{N-1}} B^{s_N}_{\alpha_{N-1}}
\end{align}</math>.

As the result,

:<math>\psi_{s_1...s_N} = \sum_{\alpha_1, \ldots,\alpha_{N}} A^{s_1}_{\alpha_1} A^{s_2}_{\alpha_1,\alpha_2}\ldots A^{s_{n}}_{\alpha_{n-1},\alpha_{n}} D_{\alpha_n, \alpha_n}B^{s_{n+1}}_{\alpha_n, \alpha_{n+1}} B^{s_{n+2}}_{\alpha_{n+1},\alpha_{n+2}}\ldots B^{s_{N-1}}_{\alpha_{N-2},\alpha_{N-1}} B^{s_N}_{\alpha_{N-1}} </math>.

== Examples ==

=== Greenberger–Horne–Zeilinger state ===
[[Greenberger–Horne–Zeilinger state]], which for {{math|<var>N</var>}} particles can be written as [[Quantum superposition|superposition]] of {{math|<var>N</var>}} zeros and {{math|<var>N</var>}} ones 
:<math>|\mathrm{GHZ}\rangle = \frac{|0\rangle^{\otimes N} + |1\rangle^{\otimes N}}{\sqrt{2}}</math>
can be expressed as a Matrix Product State, up to normalization, with
:<math>
A^{(0)} =
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0\\
0 & 0
\end{bmatrix}
\quad
A^{(1)} =
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & 0\\
0 & 1
\end{bmatrix},
</math>
or equivalently, using notation from:<ref name="Crosswhite:2008" />
:<math>
A =
\begin{bmatrix}
| 0 \rangle & 0\\
0 & | 1 \rangle
\end{bmatrix}.
</math>

This notation uses matrices with entries being state vectors (instead of complex numbers), and when [[matrix multiplication|multiplying matrices]] using [[tensor product]] for its entries (instead of product of two complex numbers). Such matrix is constructed as
:<math>A \equiv | 0 \rangle A^{(0)} + | 1 \rangle A^{(1)} + \ldots + | d-1 \rangle A^{(d-1)}.</math>
Note that tensor product is not [[commutative property|commutative]].

In this particular example, a product of two ''A'' matrices is:
:<math>
A A=
\begin{bmatrix}
| 0 0 \rangle & 0\\
0 & | 1 1 \rangle
\end{bmatrix}.
</math>

=== W state ===
[[W state]], i.e., the superposition of all the computational basis states of [[Hamming weight]] one.
: <math>|\mathrm{W}\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(|001\rangle + |010\rangle + |100\rangle)</math>

Even though the state is permutation-symmetric, its simplest MPS representation is not.<ref name="PerezGarcia:2006" /> For example:
:<math>
A_1 =
\begin{bmatrix}
| 0 \rangle  & 0\\
| 0 \rangle & | 1 \rangle
\end{bmatrix}
\quad
A_2 =
\begin{bmatrix}
| 0 \rangle  & | 1 \rangle\\
0 & | 0 \rangle
\end{bmatrix}
\quad
A_3 =
\begin{bmatrix}
| 1 \rangle & 0\\
0 & | 0 \rangle
\end{bmatrix}.
</math>

=== AKLT model ===
{{Main|AKLT model}}

The AKLT [[ground state]] wavefunction, which is the historical example of MPS approach,<ref name=Affleck:1987 />  corresponds to the choice<ref name="Schollwoeck:2011" />

: <math>A^{+} = \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\ \sigma^{+}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & \sqrt{2/3}\\
0 & 0
\end{bmatrix}
</math>

: <math>A^{0} = \frac{-1}{\sqrt{3}}\ \sigma^{z}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
-1/\sqrt{3} & 0\\
0 & 1/\sqrt{3}
\end{bmatrix}
</math>

: <math>A^{-} = -\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\ \sigma^{-}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & 0\\
-\sqrt{2/3} & 0
\end{bmatrix}
</math>

where the <math>\sigma\text{'s}</math> are [[Pauli matrices]], or 
: <math>
A =
\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}
\begin{bmatrix}
- | 0 \rangle  & \sqrt{2} | + \rangle\\
- \sqrt{2} | - \rangle & | 0 \rangle
\end{bmatrix}.
</math>

=== Majumdar–Ghosh model ===
{{Main|Majumdar–Ghosh model}}

Majumdar–Ghosh ground state can be written as MPS with

:<math>
A =
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & \left| \uparrow \right\rangle & \left| \downarrow \right\rangle \\
\frac{-1}{\sqrt{2}} \left| \downarrow \right\rangle & 0 & 0 \\
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \left| \uparrow \right\rangle & 0 & 0
\end{bmatrix}.
</math>
